exam: What bedside signs differentiate SVCS from simple facial oedema? — Look for distended chest‑wall veins, worsening when supine, and upper‑body cyanosis.

A patient with known HIV presents with facial swelling and a mediastinal mass on X‑ray. What is your next diagnostic step? — Obtain tissue diagnosis (biopsy) because lymphoma is likely and guides therapy.
Why is immediate radiotherapy preferred over chemotherapy in a patient with small‑cell lung cancer causing SVCS? — Radiotherapy provides faster tumour shrinkage, relieving obstruction within days.
A patient with a recent central line develops SVCS. Which treatment is first‑line and why? — Anticoagulation to dissolve thrombus; steroids are added only if there is surrounding inflammation.
How would you manage SVCS in a hospital without CT capability? — Use chest X‑ray, bedside ultrasound, and start empirical steroids while arranging transfer for definitive imaging.
What complication should you monitor for after starting high‑dose steroids in SVCS? — Hyperglycaemia and increased infection risk, especially in HIV/TB patients.
Explain why head‑of‑bed elevation improves symptoms. — It reduces venous pressure in the SVC territory, decreasing facial and neck swelling.
When is surgical bypass of the SVC indicated? — When obstruction is refractory to medical therapy, the tumour is not radiosensitive, and the patient has a good performance status.
ai.title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Obstruction of the superior vena cava causes venous congestion of the head, neck and upper limbs. In low‑resource settings the most common causes are malignancy and infection. Prompt recognition and relief of the obstruction are essential.

b: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging that shows a narrowed SVC and a mediastinal mass or thrombus.
sections.p: Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is a clinical syndrome of impaired venous return from the upper body due to partial or complete obstruction of the superior vena cava.

t.b: Does a mediastinal widening or mass exist? – Positive suggests external compression; a normal film does not exclude SVCS.

t.a: Contrast‑enhanced CT chest (if CT scanner available)
t.b: What is the cause and level of obstruction? – Shows mass, lymphadenopathy, or intraluminal thrombus; guides further management.
Is there thrombosis of the internal jugular or subclavian veins? – Positive supports a thrombotic cause; negative does not rule out central obstruction.

b: Mild: facial swelling, mild dyspnoea, no respiratory compromise.
Moderate: prominent facial/neck edema, cough, dysphagia, orthopnoea.
Severe (life‑threatening): stridor, cerebral oedema, hypotension, rapid progression.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and hemodynamic impact.

b: Bronchogenic carcinoma (especially small‑cell) – most common worldwide.
Non‑Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., Burkitt, diffuse large B‑cell) – frequent in HIV patients.
Tuberculous mediastinal lymphadenitis – common in TB endemic areas.
Thrombus from indwelling central venous catheters or pacemaker leads.
Mediastinal germ‑cell tumours (young men).
sections.p: In East Africa the aetiology reflects local disease prevalence and limited oncology services.

b: Facial plethora, periorbital oedema, and cyanosis that worsen when supine.
Distended neck and chest wall veins, especially over the clavicles.
Dyspnoea, cough, hoarseness, and dysphagia from airway or oesophageal compression.
Headache, visual disturbance, or altered mental status if cerebral venous pressure rises.
sections.p: Patients develop signs of venous congestion above the heart.
Imaging confirms obstruction and identifies the cause; basic labs assess fitness for treatment.

t.b: Is the patient immunocompromised or anaemic? – Guides choice of chemotherapy or anti‑TB therapy.
Are kidneys safe for contrast or nephrotoxic drugs? – Determines whether CT contrast can be used.

t.a: Fine‑needle aspiration / biopsy of accessible mass
t.b: What is the histology? – Determines definitive therapy (chemo, radiotherapy, anti‑TB).

b: Airway collapse with stridor or severe hypoxia.
Cerebral oedema causing seizures or coma.
Superior vena cava rupture (rare, usually after invasive procedures).
sections.p: Unrelieved obstruction can rapidly become fatal.

b: Elevate head of bed 30–45°; give supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ < 94%.
Steroids (e.g., dexamethasone) to reduce oedema when a tumour is suspected.
Radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours (small‑cell lung cancer, lymphoma) when rapid relief is needed.
Anticoagulation (e.g., low‑molecular‑weight heparin) for thrombotic SVCS; avoid if active bleeding.
Chemotherapy for chemosensitive lymphomas or germ‑cell tumours; start promptly after tissue diagnosis.
Anti‑TB therapy for tuberculous lymphadenitis; monitor for drug interactions with steroids.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause while providing symptomatic relief and protecting the airway.

b: Repeat imaging 4–6 weeks after definitive therapy to ensure recanalisation.
Educate patients with central lines on early signs of thrombosis.
Vaccinate HIV‑positive patients and provide TB prophylaxis where indicated.
sections.p: After acute control, monitor for recurrence and manage the primary disease.

b: Angioedema – rapid onset, usually drug‑related, no neck vein distension.
Heart failure with superior vena cava overload – peripheral oedema is bilateral, not limited to head/neck.
Superior mediastinal syndrome from aortic arch aneurysm – pulsatile mass, often painful.
sections.p: Conditions that also cause facial swelling and upper‑body venous congestion.

b: Chest X‑ray can be normal in early SVCS; a normal film should not delay CT if clinical suspicion is high.
D‑dimer may be normal in catheter‑related thrombus; reliance on it can miss the diagnosis.
sections.p: Some investigations may appear normal despite serious obstruction.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening facial swelling with neurological changes
Hypotension or signs of cerebral oedema
